teaser: Buried three times, once by professors who were afraid of her. Meet the Aztec mother of the gods.
review_notes:
'Buried three times': after the conquest (date undocumented, inferred), reburied at the university soon after 1790, reburied again after being shown to Humboldt in 1803; definitively unearthed in the 1820s.
Height given here as about 2.5 m (sources vary between 2.52 and 2.7 m) and weight about 3 tons: please check.
Discovery date 13 August 1790 near the Zócalo.
Identification as Coatlicue is traditional; some scholars propose other readings (e.g. a tzitzimitl).
The relief of Tlaltecuhtli under the base is not visible in the photo.
Catalog year 1500 is approximate.

lesson.text: Three. That is how many times this statue has been put underground. Once after the Spanish conquest of Mexico, and twice more after it was found again in 1790, by educated men who decided it was better not to look at it.

She is called Coatlicue, “Serpent Skirt” in Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs. She was carved around 1500 in Tenochtitlan, the island capital that lies under today's Mexico City. She stands about 2.5 meters high (over 8 feet), cut from one block of andesite, a gray volcanic stone.

Give your eyes a second to sort her out, because nothing is where you expect. The first shock is at the top. There is a face, with two round eyes and a row of fangs. Now check what that face is made of.

lesson.title: A head that is not one
lesson.text: Start at the top of the block and work out how the “face” is built.

spots.title: One eye, one snake
spots.text: This round eye belongs to a snake seen in profile, its snout pointing toward the center. Scales in small squares cover its head.

spots.title: Its mirror image
spots.text: A second snake faces the first, nose to nose. Together their two profiles add up to one frontal face. She has been beheaded, and the snakes are her blood.

spots.title: Fangs and tongue
spots.text: Curved fangs meet in the middle and a forked tongue hangs down, split in two flaps. The mouth belongs to both snakes at once.

lesson.text: In Aztec carving, snakes springing from a wound mean streams of blood. So this is a body whose head has been cut off, and whose life is pouring out as two serpents. The same thing happens at the shoulders: her arms end in snake heads too.

The Aztecs told that Coatlicue was sweeping a temple on Snake Mountain when a ball of feathers fell from the sky. She tucked it into her waistband and became pregnant with Huitzilopochtli, the god of sun and war.

Her other children, ashamed, marched against her. In the best-known version Huitzilopochtli is born fully armed and defeats them. Some scholars think the statue shows another ending, in which the mother is killed, and her sacrifice sets the sun in motion.
For the Aztecs, death was not the opposite of life but its fuel. Coatlicue is terrifying and motherly at once: the earth that swallows everything and gives birth to everything.
The sculptor organized all this horror with strict order. Step back from the details and the statue turns out to be as calculated as a building, with an axis, a crossbar and a clear outline.
Three lines show how firmly the block is planned.

lines.label: The mirror
lines.text: Fold the statue along this line and the halves match: snake for snake, hand for hand, claw for claw. Symmetry gives her the stillness of a monument.

lines.label: The arms
lines.text: The bent arms push out to both sides at shoulder height, each ending in a snake head. Crossed with the vertical, they give the block the shape of a cross.

lines.label: A leaning mass
lines.text: The outline stays close to the original block. In profile the figure also leans forward, so she looms over anyone standing in front of her.

lesson.text: That lean matters. Worshippers did not view her from a comfortable distance in a museum. She rose above them in or near the great temple precinct, probably painted in strong colors, tilting toward them like something about to fall.
Now the chest. She wears a necklace that no jeweler made: open human hands and human hearts, strung in alternation. And at the center, where a pendant would hang, something looks straight at you.
The pendant of her necklace doubles as her belt buckle. Find it.

spots.title: The skull
spots.text: A human skull with round, wide-open eyes, as if still alive. Around it you can see open hands with every finger carved, palms out, and above them the rounded hearts.

lesson.text: Under her feet, on the base that touches the ground, the sculptors carved a full relief of the earth deity Tlaltecuhtli. Nobody was ever meant to see it. It was made for the earth itself.

In 1521 the Spanish took Tenochtitlan and tore down its temples. At some point the statue ended up underground. It lay there until August 13, 1790, when workers laying drains in the main square of Mexico City struck stone.

It was moved to the courtyard of the university. The professors soon had it buried again. They feared it would give students wrong ideas and, worse, that Indigenous people would come to honor it. Some reportedly did, leaving candles and flowers.

In 1803 the German explorer Alexander von Humboldt asked to see her. She was dug up so he could study and draw her, and when he had finished she was covered with earth once more. She came out for good only after Mexico's independence.

spots.title: The skirt
spots.text: The skirt that gives her her name: rattlesnakes braided together like wickerwork, their scales cut as a grid of small diamonds.

spots.title: A snake for an arm
spots.text: At the edge of the block, the raised arm ends in a broad serpent head instead of a hand. The other side mirrors it.

spots.title: An open hand
spots.text: A severed hand, palm out, thumb up. The fingers are neat and fleshy, carved with real attention to anatomy.

spots.title: A heart
spots.text: This rounded form with ridges is a human heart, the most precious offering in Aztec ritual.

spots.title: Between the legs
spots.text: A thick snake hangs down between her legs, below the skirt, on a ground of cut patterns.

spots.title: The feet
spots.text: Not human feet but great clawed paws, gripping the ground. Round eyes are carved on them.

lesson.text: Today she stands in the main Aztec hall of the Museo Nacional de Antropología, no longer hidden, and Mexican artists from Diego Rivera onward have claimed her as an ancestor. The fear she inspired in 1790 has turned into something closer to pride.

quiz.question: What does the name Coatlicue mean?
What is her “face” actually made of?
options: Two snakes meeting nose to nose
quiz.explanation: Two serpent profiles combine into one frontal face.

quiz.question: In Aztec carving, what do snakes springing from a wound stand for?
quiz.explanation: They show blood gushing from a beheaded body.

quiz.question: Why did university professors rebury the statue after 1790?
options: They feared it would revive the old worship
It was too heavy for the floor
They wanted to protect it from rain
quiz.explanation: They worried Indigenous people would honor it again.

quiz.question: What hangs on her necklace?
options: Human hands and hearts, with a skull
quiz.explanation: Hands and hearts alternate around a central skull.

quiz.question: What is carved under the statue's base?
options: A relief of the earth deity Tlaltecuhtli
quiz.explanation: The hidden underside carries a full relief no one was meant to see.

facts.text: Coatlicue was discovered by workers laying drains in Mexico City in 1790.
facts.explanation: She was struck by workers in the main square on August 13, 1790.

facts.text: The statue is assembled from dozens of small stones.
facts.explanation: It is carved from a single block of andesite.

facts.text: Humboldt took the statue back to Germany.
facts.explanation: He only studied and drew it; it was reburied in Mexico afterward.
